subject: Vocabulary
topic: Words from law and legal usage — mixed tiers
description: Plaintiff, defendant, verdict, perjury, acquittal, alibi, indictment — exam-frequent

questions.stem: In a civil suit, the PLAINTIFF is the person who:

options.option_text: Defends the case in front of the trial judge
Initiates the legal action by filing the suit
Records witness statements in the courtroom
Reads out the final verdict in open court

questions.explanation: PLAINTIFF — the party who FILES a civil suit. The opposing party is the DEFENDANT. In criminal cases, the equivalent of the plaintiff is the PROSECUTION (state). Distractor 1 = the defendant. Distractor 3 = court reporter / stenographer. Distractor 4 = the judge.

questions.stem: PERJURY is the criminal offence of:

options.option_text: Refusing to answer a question put by a magistrate
Wilfully telling a lie under oath in a legal proceeding
Disobeying a lawful court order made by the bench
Bribing a witness to favourably testify in court

questions.explanation: PERJURY — knowingly false statement under oath. Indian Penal Code Section 191-193 criminalises perjury. Sentence up to 7 years + fine. Distractor 1 = contempt or refusal-to-testify, different offence. Distractor 3 = contempt of court. Distractor 4 = subornation (bribing a witness, distinct offence).

questions.stem: An ACQUITTAL is a court verdict that:

options.option_text: Convicts the accused and imposes a prison sentence
Declares the accused not guilty of the alleged charges
Sends the case to a higher court for fresh review
Postpones the hearing to a later scheduled date

questions.explanation: ACQUITTAL — finding of NOT GUILTY by the court. The accused is then released and cannot be tried again for the same offence (double-jeopardy bar — Article 20(2) of the Constitution + Section 300 CrPC). Distractor 1 = conviction. Distractor 3 = appeal / remand. Distractor 4 = adjournment.

questions.stem: An ALIBI is a defence used by an accused person to show that:

options.option_text: Another known person also committed a similar crime
He was elsewhere when the alleged crime was committed
The crime was committed in self-defence under threat
The witness against him is biased or unreliable

questions.explanation: ALIBI — Latin 'alibi' (elsewhere). The accused proves he was at a DIFFERENT location when the crime occurred → cannot have done it. Burden of proof is on the accused (to a preponderance, not beyond reasonable doubt). Section 11 of Indian Evidence Act allows alibi evidence. Distractor 1 = alternative-suspect theory. Distractor 3 = self-defence plea. Distractor 4 = challenge to witness credibility.

questions.stem: An AFFIDAVIT is most accurately described as:

options.option_text: An informal letter written from one party to another
A written statement of facts sworn before a notary or magistrate
A copy of an original document attested as a true copy
An order issued by a higher court to a lower court

questions.explanation: AFFIDAVIT — written sworn statement. Must be sworn before an authorised official (notary public / magistrate / oath commissioner). Used widely in Indian courts and admin to verify facts under penalty of perjury. Distractor 1 = informal letter / private correspondence. Distractor 3 = ATTESTED copy or certified copy. Distractor 4 = writ / order.

options.option_text: Apology issued to the court before sentencing
Charge accusing a person of a serious criminal offence
Out-of-court agreement settling a civil dispute
Pardon granted by the executive head of the state

questions.explanation: INDICTMENT — formal accusation, usually presented by a prosecutor (or a grand jury in US). Sets out the criminal charges the accused must answer. In India, the equivalent is the 'chargesheet' (filed by police / investigating agency under Section 173 CrPC) and 'framing of charges' by the trial court. Distractor 1 = apology / mitigation. Distractor 3 = settlement / compromise. Distractor 4 = clemency / pardon (Article 72 / Article 161).

questions.stem: BAIL is the temporary release of an arrested person, typically on:

options.option_text: A pardon from the head of the state in question
A bond or surety guaranteeing the accused's later appearance
Acquittal by the trial judge after first hearing
Settlement of the alleged offence outside the courtroom

questions.explanation: BAIL — temporary release pending trial; the accused signs a bond (and/or sureties stand guarantee) promising to appear when summoned. In India regulated by Cr.P.C. (and now BNSS, 2023). 'Bailable' offences — bail is a right; 'non-bailable' — court's discretion. ANTICIPATORY BAIL (Section 438 Cr.P.C.) — before arrest. Distractor 1 = pardon (clemency, Article 72/161). Distractor 3 = acquittal (final). Distractor 4 = compounding / settlement (separate concept).

questions.stem: A SUBPOENA is a legal writ that compels a person to:

options.option_text: pay a fine imposed by the court for contempt
appear before a court or produce documents as ordered
surrender their passport pending trial in a criminal case
accept a plea bargain offered by the prosecution party

questions.explanation: A subpoena (Latin: 'under penalty') is a court writ commanding a person to attend proceedings or produce documents under threat of punishment for non-compliance. Option A confuses it with a fine order; Option C describes a travel restriction, not a subpoena.

questions.stem: In legal usage, JURISDICTION most precisely refers to:

options.option_text: the penalty imposed on a convicted offender by a judge
the formal authority of a court to hear and decide cases
the process of questioning witnesses before a trial begins
the written record of proceedings maintained by the court

questions.explanation: Jurisdiction (Latin: 'juris dictio' — to speak the law) denotes the legal authority vested in a court to adjudicate matters within a defined territory or subject matter. Option C describes pre-trial deposition; Option D describes court records or minutes.

questions.stem: A person is said to be in CONTEMPT OF COURT when they:

options.option_text: challenge a court verdict through a formal higher appeal
wilfully disobey a court order or disrespect its authority
submit fabricated evidence in support of their own defence
refuse to engage the services of a court-appointed counsel

questions.explanation: Contempt of court covers both civil contempt (disobeying court orders) and criminal contempt (scandalising court authority). Option A is a lawful right — filing an appeal is not contempt. Option C is perjury or fabrication of evidence, a separate offence.

questions.stem: In civil law, a TORT is best described as:

options.option_text: a breach of a written contractual obligation between two parties
a civil wrong causing harm that entitles the victim to damages
an agreement reached between disputing parties to avoid litigation
a criminal act punishable by imprisonment under the penal code

questions.explanation: Tort (French: 'wrong') is a civil wrong independent of contract — e.g., negligence, defamation, nuisance — for which courts award damages. Option A is a contractual breach (a separate civil claim). Option D errs by classifying tort as criminal, which it is not.

questions.stem: A court issues a WRIT OF HABEAS CORPUS primarily to:

options.option_text: order a government official to perform a specific public duty
direct the custodian to produce a detained person before court
prohibit a lower court from exceeding its defined legal authority
transfer a pending case from a lower court to a higher court

questions.explanation: Habeas corpus (Latin: 'you shall have the body') is a safeguard against unlawful detention; it requires the detaining authority to present the person before court and justify the custody. Option A describes mandamus; Option C describes prohibition; Option D describes certiorari.

questions.stem: An AMICUS CURIAE in court proceedings is best described as:

options.option_text: a witness summoned by the court to supply expert technical testimony
a party or body not in the suit who assists the court with expertise
the public prosecutor appointed by the state to argue criminal cases
a court-appointed guardian representing the interests of a minor party

questions.explanation: Amicus curiae (Latin: 'friend of the court') is a non-party — often an NGO, expert body, or senior advocate — who files a brief to aid the court on complex legal or public-interest questions. Unlike an expert witness (Option A), the amicus is not under oath and is not summoned by either party.

questions.stem: An EX PARTE order in legal proceedings refers to an order:

options.option_text: granted jointly after two courts exercise concurrent jurisdiction over one matter
made by a court on the application of one party without notifying the other
passed unanimously by a full bench on a pressing constitutional question
issued by a tribunal whose decision has been appealed to a superior court

questions.explanation: Ex parte (Latin: 'from one side') describes a court action taken at the request of, and for the benefit of, one party in the absence of and without notice to the other — common in urgent injunctions. Candidates confuse it with in absentia (trial in absence of accused) or suo motu proceedings; both differ structurally from ex parte.
